claim: Brainstem olivocochlear neurons (OCNs) modulate the earliest stages of auditory processing through feedback projections to the cochlea.
source: Brainstem olivocochlear neurons (OCNs) modulate the earliest stages of auditory processing through feedback projections to the cochlea and have been shown to influence hearing and protect the ear from sound-induced damage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of OCNs.

claim: OCNs have been shown to influence hearing and protect the ear from sound-induced damage.
source: Brainstem olivocochlear neurons (OCNs) modulate the earliest stages of auditory processing through feedback projections to the cochlea and have been shown to influence hearing and protect the ear from sound-induced damage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about OCN function.

claim: Single-nucleus sequencing, anatomical reconstructions, and electrophysiology were used to characterize murine OCNs during postnatal development, in mature animals, and after sound exposure.
source: Here, we used single-nucleus sequencing, anatomical reconstructions, and electrophysiology to characterize murine OCNs during postnatal development, in mature animals, and after sound exposure.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Markers for known medial (MOC) and lateral (LOC) OCN subtypes were identified.
source: We identified markers for known medial (MOC) and lateral (LOC) OCN subtypes, and show that they express distinct cohorts of physiologically relevant genes that change over development.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MOC and LOC subtypes express distinct cohorts of physiologically relevant genes that change over development.
source: We identified markers for known medial (MOC) and lateral (LOC) OCN subtypes, and show that they express distinct cohorts of physiologically relevant genes that change over development.
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis across developmental timepoints shown in the manuscript.

claim: A neuropeptide-enriched LOC subtype that produces Neuropeptide Y along with other neurotransmitters was discovered.
source: In addition, we discovered a neuropeptide-enriched LOC subtype that produces Neuropeptide Y along with other neurotransmitters.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the sub-clustering analysis and immunostaining experiments.

claim: Both LOC subtypes extend arborizations over wide frequency domains throughout the cochlea.
source: Throughout the cochlea, both LOC subtypes extend arborizations over wide frequency domains.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical reconstructions of individual LOC axons.

claim: LOC neuropeptide expression is strongly upregulated days after acoustic trauma.
source: Moreover, LOC neuropeptide expression is strongly upregulated days after acoustic trauma, potentially providing a sustained protective signal to the cochlea.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sound exposure experiments showing increased peptide expression.

claim: OCNs are poised to have diffuse, dynamic effects on early auditory processing over timescales ranging from milliseconds to days.
source: OCNs are therefore poised to have diffuse, dynamic effects on early auditory processing over timescales ranging from milliseconds to days.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined findings of widespread anatomical projections and experience-dependent peptide expression changes.

claim: A small group of several hundred olivocochlear neurons (OCNs) in the superior olivary complex (SOC) extend projections to the cochlea.
source: Analogously, a small group of several hundred olivocochlear neurons (OCNs) in the superior olivary complex (SOC) extend projections all the way to the peripheral hearing organ, the cochlea, enabling direct regulation of initial detection and encoding of auditory stimuli (Rasmussen, 1946; Rasmussen, 1953; Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by historical citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: OCNs enable direct regulation of initial detection and encoding of auditory stimuli.
source: Analogously, a small group of several hundred olivocochlear neurons (OCNs) in the superior olivary complex (SOC) extend projections all the way to the peripheral hearing organ, the cochlea, enabling direct regulation of initial detection and encoding of auditory stimuli (Rasmussen, 1946; Rasmussen, 1953; Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: OCNs integrate information from both ascending auditory pathways and descending central circuits.
source: By integrating information from both ascending auditory pathways and descending central circuits, OCNs serve as a conduit for an animal's experiences and needs to modulate sound information at the earliest stages of sensory processing.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about OCN function based on established knowledge.

claim: The dataset includes 45,828 nuclei from 61 animals across three ages.
source: After filtering out low-quality cells and infrequently expressed genes (see Materials and methods), our dataset includes 45,828 nuclei: 16,753 cells from P1 animals; 15,542 from P5 animals; and 13,533 cells from P26–P28 animals.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset composition.

claim: Unsupervised, graph-based clustering analysis identified 56 clusters.
source: Unsupervised, graph-based clustering analysis identified 56 clusters (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the computational analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Each neuronal cluster includes cells from all three timepoints.
source: Each neuronal cluster includes cells from all three timepoints (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Two OCN clusters were identified based on expression of Gata3.
source: Among these, two OCN clusters were identified based on expression of Gata3, which is expressed in OCNs but not in canonical motor neuron populations (Figure 1H; Karis et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data shown in Figure 1H and a citation.

claim: LOC and MOC clusters were identified by expression of Urocortin (Ucn) and Atp1a3, respectively.
source: LOC and MOC clusters were identified by expression of the LOC-specific peptide Urocortin (Ucn) (Kaiser et al., 2011; Figure 1I) and the Na,K-ATPase Atp1a3, which is expressed in MOCs but not LOCs in mature rats (McLean et al., 2009; Figure 1J).
evidence: This is based on known markers from the literature and confirmed in the sequencing data.

claim: OCNs show selective expression of Cadps2.
source: For instance, OCNs show selective expression of Cadps2, which encodes the calcium-dependent activator protein for secretion 2 (CADPS2, also known as CAPS-2; Figure 1K).
evidence: This is shown in the sequencing data in Figure 1K.

claim: CADPS2 is a member of the Munc13 and CAPS family of priming proteins.
source: CADPS2 is a member of the Munc13 and CAPS family of priming proteins (Imig et al., 2014; Jockusch et al., 2007; Nestvogel et al., 2020) and has been linked to exocytosis of dense-core vesicles (Tandon et al., 1998; Speidel et al., 2003; Grishanin et al., 2004; Renden et al., 2001), consistent with neuropeptide release from OCNs (Eybalin, 1993; Kitcher et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge from multiple citations.

claim: Fluorescent in situ hybridization confirmed that Cadps2 is expressed in both MOCs and LOCs but is not detectable in FMNs.
source: Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) in P27–P28 mice confirmed that Cadps2 is expressed in both MOCs and LOCs but is not detectable in FMNs (Figure 1L and M; n=3 animals).
evidence: This is validated by FISH experiments shown in Figure 1L and M.

claim: Col4a4 is expressed in virtually all LOCs in mature animals.
source: We found that Col4a4 is expressed in virtually all LOCs in mature (P26–P28) animals, whereas Zfp804a is expressed in virtually all MOCs (Figure 2B–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FISH validation shown in Figure 2.

claim: Zfp804a is expressed in virtually all MOCs in mature animals.
source: We found that Col4a4 is expressed in virtually all LOCs in mature (P26–P28) animals, whereas Zfp804a is expressed in virtually all MOCs (Figure 2B–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FISH validation shown in Figure 2.

claim: LOCs and MOCs differ in expression of genes encoding transcription factors, adhesion molecules, and receptors and ion channels.
source: Despite their early shared origins, FMNs and OCNs express unique combinations of genes encoding transcription factors, adhesion molecules, and other receptors needed for proper neuronal migration, targeting, and synaptic specificity.
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2H-J.

claim: Both MOCs and LOCs generate transcripts corresponding to receptors for numerous neurotransmitters, including GABA, Glycine, acetylcholine, and glutamate.
source: Both MOCs and LOCs generate transcripts corresponding to receptors for numerous neurotransmitters, including GABA (K), Glycine (L), acetylcholine (M), and glutamate (O).
evidence: This is shown in the violin plots in Figure 2K-O.

claim: MOCs and LOCs express genes for different subunits or classes of receptors in several cases.
source: In several cases, however, MOCs and LOCs express genes for different subunits or classes of receptors (L, M, O).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2L, M, and O.

claim: Sub-clustering of mature OCNs revealed five OCN clusters.
source: This analysis revealed five OCN clusters (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the UMAP plot in Figure 3A.

claim: Two main clusters of LOCs were identified: LOC1 (242 cells) and LOC2 (75 cells).
source: Based on expression of MOC and LOC markers, we identified a large cluster of MOCs (230 cells) (Figure 3B) and two main clusters of LOCs (242 LOC1 cells, 75 LOC2 cells; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the sub-clustering analysis in Figure 3.

claim: LOC2s are distinguished by upregulation of genes for the neuropeptides CGRP (Calca), CGRP-II (Calcb), NPY, and Ucn.
source: Comparison of the two LOC subtypes revealed that LOC2s are distinguished by upregulation of genes for the neuropeptides CGRP (Calca), CGRP-II (Calcb), NPY, and Ucn (Figure 3D and J-M).
evidence: This is shown in the differential expression analysis in Figure 3D and J-M.

claim: LOC1s and LOC2s differ in expression of genes for the transcription factor Meis1 and for guidance and adhesion molecules.
source: LOC1s and LOC2s also differ in expression of the genes for the transcription factor Meis1 and for guidance and adhesion molecules, such as Tenm2, Tenm3, Unc5c, and Epha6 (Figure 3E–I), suggesting that these clusters indeed represent distinct cell types rather than reflecting the same pool of cells in different states.
evidence: This is shown in the violin plots in Figure 3E-I.

claim: LOC2s are confined to the medial wing of the LSO.
source: Consistent with this idea, LOC2s are confined to the medial wing of the LSO (n=4 animals of either sex, P28–P32), as revealed by immunostaining for CGRP and Ucn in tissue from an Npy-GFP reporter mouse (Figure 3O).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 3O.

claim: NPY seems to be a particularly reliable marker for LOC2s.
source: NPY seems to be a particularly reliable marker for LOC2s, as Ucn was not always expressed in NPY+ cells and very few cells expressed only Ucn.
evidence: This is based on the quantification of co-expression shown in Figure 3N and Supplementary file 1.

claim: An intersectional genetic approach using NpyFlpO; ChatCre; Rosa26FLTG recapitulates the pattern of NPY+ LOC restriction to the medial wing of the LSO.
source: Furthermore, an intersectional genetic approach in which NpyFlpO; ChatCre drives expression of the dual recombinase Rosa26FLTG reporter recapitulates the pattern of NPY+ LOC restriction to the medial wing of the LSO (Figure 3P), without labeling MOCs in the VNTB (arrowheads, Figure 3P) or the lateral wing of the LSO (n=4 animals of either sex, P28–P30).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the genetic labeling shown in Figure 3P.

claim: Transcripts for Penk or Pdyn were not detected in any LOC subtype by sequencing or FISH.
source: However, we were unable to observe expression of either Penk or Pdyn in any LOC subtype in either our sequencing data or via FISH (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: NPY+ LOC axons span the entirety of the base-to-apex length of the cochlea.
source: However, although the density of presumptive LOC2 axons, labeled by NpyFlpO; ChatCre; Rosa26FLTG, decreases from high-frequency (basal) to low-frequency (apical) regions, NPY+ LOC axons span the entirety of the base-to-apex length (Figure 3Q, left to right).
evidence: This is shown in the cochlear wholemount images in Figure 3Q.

claim: Ret is expressed by all OCNs from early in development.
source: To analyze the morphology and synaptic connectivity of individual OCN axons, we leveraged our discovery that Ret is expressed by all OCNs from early in development (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B) and used low doses of tamoxifen in RetCreER mice to drive expression of the Cre-dependent Igs7GFP reporter in a small number of OCNs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D; Luo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Sparsely labeled MOC axons have terminal morphologies consistent with prior dye-labeling studies.
source: Sparsely labeled MOC axons (n=40 axons, N=9 animals of both sexes) have terminal morphologies consistent with prior dye-labeling studies (Brown, 2011; Brown, 1987; Robertson and Gummer, 1985; Brown, 2014), including relatively simple axons with little-to-no branching beneath the OHCs (Figure 4A" and B); branching in the OSL (Figure 4C); complex branching beneath IHCs and among OHCs (Figure 4D) or branching in a goal-post fashion (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reconstructions in Figure 4 and supported by citations.

claim: Labeled MOCs show a slight preference for innervating the third row of OHCs.
source: Labeled MOCs show a slight preference for innervating the third row of OHCs, with 21.4% of Syp puncta in row 1, 31.6% in row 2, and 47% in row 3.
evidence: This is quantified from the MOC axon reconstructions.

claim: 45% of the reconstructed MOC axons have Syp puncta in the inner spiral bundle (ISB).
source: Additionally, 45% of the reconstructed MOC axons (18/40) have Syp puncta in the inner spiral bundle (ISB), localized among SGN peripheral fibers, either en passant (Figure 4A") or, less frequently, at terminal endings (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is quantified from the MOC axon reconstructions shown in Figure 4.

claim: There were no significant differences in the frequency of innervation or number of branch points between terminal MOC axons that did and did not contain Syp puncta in the ISB.
source: Likewise, when considering the entire dataset, there were no significant differences in the frequency of innervation (Figure 4G) or number of branch points (Figure 4H) between terminal MOC axons that did and did not contain Syp puncta in the ISB.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Individual MOCs can produce projections with variable morphologies and synaptic targets.
source: Collectively, these observations indicate that individual MOCs can produce projections with variable morphologies and synaptic targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of multiple terminal fibers from a single MOC.

claim: Genetically labeled LOC2 axons intermingle closely with parvalbumin (PV)+ SGN peripheral processes on both sides of the inner hair cell.
source: In NpyFlpO; ChatCre; Rosa26FLTG cochlea, genetically labeled LOC2 axons intermingle closely with parvalbumin (PV)+ SGN peripheral processes on both sides of the inner hair cell, although there was a qualitative bias to the modiolar side (Figure 5B), similar to what has been reported for LOCs in general (Hua et al., 2021; Liberman et al., 1990).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and supported by citations.

claim: NPY distribution was punctate and heterogeneous not just between axons, but also within individual axons.
source: NPY distribution was punctate and heterogeneous not just between axons, but also within individual axons, raising the possibility that individual LOC fibers may vary in the signaling molecules released at specific synaptic sites.
evidence: This is observed in the LOC axon reconstructions.

claim: The majority of reconstructed LOC axons had both NPY+ and NPY- Syp puncta that were present both on and off CALB2+ targets.
source: Far from falling into distinct categories, the majority of reconstructed LOC axons had both NPY+ and NPY- Syp puncta that were present both on and off CALB2+ targets (e.g. Figure 5I, K, and L).
evidence: This is shown in the LOC axon reconstructions in Figure 5.

claim: Individual LOC axons can weave from the pillar to modiolar side and extend branches that make pre-synaptic contacts on SGN peripheral processes on both sides of the IHC.
source: Indeed, individual LOC axons can weave from the pillar to modiolar side and extend branches that make pre-synaptic contacts on SGN peripheral processes on both sides of the IHC (Figure 5E, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is shown in the 3D reconstructions in Figure 5E.

claim: The LOC population showed no strong correlation between the percent of NPY+ Syp puncta in an individual LOC and any metric examined.
source: This was also true of the LOC axon population as a whole, which showed no strong correlation between the percent of NPY+ Syp puncta in an individual LOC and any metric we examined (Figure 5P–U, Figure 5—figure supplement 1O–Q), including the frequency where the LOC axon enters the ISB (Figure 5Q), its tonotopic span (Figure 5R), number of branch points (Figure 5S), total number of Syp puncta (Figure 5T), selectivity for CALB2+ targets (Figure 5U), branch depth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1O), fiber density (Figure 5—figure supplement 1P), or density of Syp puncta (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analyses in Figure 5P-U and Figure 5—figure supplement 1O-Q.

claim: GFP fluorescence intensity varies in LOC neurons in Calca-GFP mice at P16-P19.
source: At these ages, the intensity of native GFP fluorescence varies in LOC neurons (Figure 6A), consistent with differences in Calca RNA and CGRP protein levels (Figure 3J and O).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No systematic differences in the physiological properties of LOCs expressing different levels of GFP were observed.
source: Although the population as a whole was heterogeneous, we observed no systematic differences in the physiological properties of LOCs expressing different levels of GFP (Figure 6, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Input resistance did not correlate with GFP intensity in LOCs.
source: The input resistance, which was measured during a step from a holding voltage of –66 mV to –76 mV, did not correlate with GFP intensity (Figure 6I, Supplementary file 3), nor did membrane capacitance measured in voltage-clamp recordings (Figure 6J, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: GFP intensity did not correlate with action potential threshold in LOCs.
source: When the membrane was held at ~–63 mV to suppress spontaneous action potentials, there was no correlation between GFP intensity and rheobase, the action potential threshold of the first evoked spike, the amplitude from baseline of the first spike evoked at rheobase, or the number of action potentials evoked by a 10 pA current injection (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is reported in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Calca, Calcb, Ucn, and NPY all increase in LOCs during the first four postnatal weeks.
source: In examining developmental changes in our sequencing data, we found that Calca, Calcb, Ucn, and NPY all increase in LOCs during the first four postnatal weeks (Figure 7A–D, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Expression of Calca is spatially and temporally dynamic in LOCs across postnatal development.
source: In contrast, expression of Calca is spatially and temporally dynamic in LOCs across postnatal development, as shown by FISH (2–3 animals per timepoint per probe) (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F.

claim: At P5/6, Calca levels are low and biased medially.
source: At P5/6, Calca levels are low and biased medially.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Calca expression increased dramatically with the onset of hearing, with high levels detected even in the lateral LSO at P12.
source: Expression increased dramatically with the onset of hearing, with high levels of transcript detected even in the lateral LSO at P12.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F.

claim: By P28, high Calca levels are again restricted medially.
source: By P28, high Calca levels are again restricted medially (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F.

claim: CGRP expression was comparable between deaf and hearing animals at P7–P8.
source: CGRP expression was comparable between deaf and hearing animals at P7–P8 (Figure 7G, I, and K; n=11 LSOs from 6 control animals, 10 LSOs from 5 Tmc1/2dKO animals), assessed both by quantifying the fraction of CGRP+ LOCs and the slope of variation in neurotransmitter levels from the medial to lateral LSO (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7G, I, and K.

claim: After the onset of hearing, the gradient of CGRP expression was significantly perturbed in deaf mice.
source: After the onset of hearing, however, the gradient of CGRP expression was significantly perturbed in deaf mice, with high CGRP levels reaching much farther into the lateral LSO (Figure 7H, J, and L; n=12 LSOs from 6 control animals, 10 LSOs from 5 Tmc1/2dKO animals).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7H, J, and L.

claim: Ucn expression was shifted, reaching farther into the lateral LSO in deaf animals compared to hearing controls.
source: Ucn expression was also shifted, reaching farther into the lateral LSO in deaf animals compared to hearing controls (Figure 7H and M, Figure 7—figure supplement 1I; n=7 control LSOs from 4 animals, 9 Tmc1/2dKO LSOs from 5 animals).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7H and M.

claim: The fraction of ChAT+ LOCs expressing TH was elevated 9 days after sound exposure.
source: As expected, the fraction of ChAT+ LOCs expressing TH was elevated 9 days after sound exposure (Figure 8A–C; n=4 exposed and 4 unexposed animals of either sex).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: An even larger increase in the fraction of LOCs expressing Ucn or NPY was observed after sound exposure.
source: In addition, we observed an even larger increase in the fraction of LOCs expressing Ucn or NPY (Figure 8A and D–G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A and D-G.

claim: The levels of CGRP increased qualitatively throughout the LSO after sound exposure.
source: Because all LOCs already express CGRP, there was no increase in the fraction of CGRP+ LOCs, although the levels of CGRP increased qualitatively throughout the LSO (Figure 8A, H, I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A, H, and I.

claim: The slope of peptide expression remained unaltered after sound exposure, with higher levels largely constrained to the medial wing.
source: Across all neuropeptides, the slope of peptide expression remained unaltered after sound exposure, with higher levels largely constrained to the medial wing (Figure 8).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claim: TH levels increased throughout the LSO after sound exposure.
source: In contrast, TH levels increased throughout the LSO, suggesting that the mechanisms driving LOCs to express TH may be different from those that govern neuropeptide expression (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: Hearing shapes the signaling repertoire of a subset of LOC neurons, both developmentally and in adults.
source: Thus, hearing shapes the signaling repertoire of a subset of LOC neurons, both developmentally and in adults.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental and sound exposure experiments.

claim: Some variant of the olivocochlear efferent system exists for all hair cell sensory systems.
source: Some variant of the olivocochlear efferent system exists for all hair cell sensory systems: groups of feedback cells project to auditory, vestibular, and lateral line neurons in all classes of vertebrates, and even some invertebrates (Roberts and Meredith, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The wide conservation of the olivocochlear system across evolutionary time suggests that OCNs play a crucial functional role.
source: The wide conservation of this circuitry across evolutionary time suggests that OCNs play a crucial functional role.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary conservation.

claim: Induced peptide expression persists for over a week after noise exposure.
source: Induced peptide expression persists for over a week after noise exposure (Figure 8), presenting a mechanism by which LOCs can modulate downstream targets on the timescale of days.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8, which examines expression 9 days after exposure.

claim: LOC1s and LOC2s vary in expression of genes that encode transcription factors and cell-adhesion molecules.
source: First, LOC1s and LOC2s vary in expression of genes that encode transcription factors and cell-adhesion molecules, attributes that are typically associated with cell types rather than cell states (Paul et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis and a citation.

claim: Peptide-high LOC2s are anatomically segregated from LOC1s.
source: Second, peptide-high LOC2s are anatomically segregated from LOC1s (Figure 3O, P).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3O and P.

claim: The medial bias in neuropeptide expression is already present by at least P5/P6, prior to the onset of hearing.
source: Moreover, the medial bias in neuropeptide expression is already present by at least P5/P6, prior to the onset of hearing, suggesting that this effect cannot be attributed to a stimulus that might preferentially activate medial LOCs, like ultrasonic vocalizations (Figure 7E, F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: NPY-expressing cells are biased to the medial LSO across perturbations, whereas cells in the far lateral LSO never express Ucn or NPY.
source: Finally, although we also show that peptide expression in LOCs can be altered by sound (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and Figure 8), NPY-expressing cells are biased to the medial LSO across perturbations, whereas cells in the far lateral LSO never express Ucn or NPY (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 8).
evidence: This is shown across multiple figures examining different conditions.

claim: Ucn and CGRP are enriched in the medial LSO of mature gerbils and rats, respectively.
source: Although LOC2s have never been specifically described in the literature, Ucn and CGRP are also enriched in the medial LSO of mature gerbils and rats, respectively, indicating that LOC1/2 differences may be conserved across species (Kaiser et al., 2011; Vetter et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in other species.

claim: Bifurcating axons did not differ from non-bifurcating axons in any anatomical metric examined.
source: Nevertheless, although we cannot be certain whether any individual LOC axons in our 3D reconstructions arise from shell or intrinsic neurons, we found that bifurcating axons—a putative marker of shell neuron identity (Warr et al., 1997)—did not differ from non-bifurcating axons in any anatomical metric we examined (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–N), indicating that the distinction between shell and intrinsic LOCs does not explain the diversity of LOC morphology present in mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J-N.

claim: The distinction between LOC1s and LOC2s is insufficient to explain LOC heterogeneity.
source: The distinction between LOC1s and LOC2s is also insufficient to explain LOC heterogeneity: we found no meaningful correlations between the fraction of NPY+ pre-synaptic puncta in LOC axons and any morphological attributes (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) or between Calca-GFP intensity and any physiological characteristics (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in the analyses in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The molecular differences that define LOC2s do not correlate with any of the physiological or peripheral morphological characteristics measured.
source: It is striking that the molecular differences that define LOC2s—as confirmed by in situ hybridization, immunostaining, and genetic labeling—do not correlate with any of the physiological or peripheral morphological characteristics that we measured.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from multiple experiments.

claim: MOCs and LOCs can be molecularly distinguished by at least P1.
source: Accordingly, MOCs and LOCs can be molecularly distinguished by at least P1, with many cell-type specific markers that persist into adulthood (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the developmental sequencing data in Figure 2.

claim: Both MOCs and LOCs downregulate several GABA receptor subunits while increasing expression of the glycine receptor subunit Glra1.
source: For example, both MOCs and LOCs downregulate several GABA receptor subunits while increasing expression of the glycine receptor subunit Glra1, indicating a transition from receiving GABAergic to glycinergic inputs (Korada and Schwartz, 1999; Kotak et al., 1998).
evidence: This is shown in the developmental gene expression data and supported by citations.

claim: LOC2 specification may happen relatively early in development, as LOC2s can be recognized as early as P5 by enriched expression of NPY and CGRP in the medial LSO.
source: As with diversification of broader OCN subtypes, LOC1/LOC2 specification may also happen relatively early in development, as LOC2s can be recognized as early as P5 by enriched expression of NPY and CGRP in the medial LSO (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: LOC2 markers such as NPY are localized medially both before and after the onset of hearing.
source: In contrast, LOC2 markers such as NPY are localized medially both before and after the onset of hearing.
evidence: This is shown in the developmental analysis in Figure 7.

claim: LOCs express Hcrtr2, which encodes an orexin receptor.
source: In keeping with this interpretation, LOCs, but not MOCs, express Hcrtr2, which encodes an orexin receptor (Figure 2Q), suggesting that LOCs may be poised to transmit information about general arousal state to the cochlea.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2Q.

claim: The duration and intensity of sound exposure affect the number of LOCs that induce TH expression.
source: Previous work found that the duration and intensity of sound exposure affect the number of LOCs that induce TH expression, with more intense stimuli inducing greater TH expression (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a citation.

claim: Recordings from SGNs show that dopamine can reduce SGN firing rates.
source: Consistent with this model, recordings from SGNs show that dopamine can reduce SGN firing rates, potentially as a way of reducing excitotoxicity evoked by loud sounds (Wu et al., 2020; Ruel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transcripts of the inhibitory, G-coupled NPY receptor Npy1r were detected in low levels in Type Ic SGNs.
source: For example, transcripts of the inhibitory, G-coupled NPY receptor Npy1r were detected in low levels in Type Ic SGNs (Shrestha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Most studies on the effects of CGRP in the inner ear of mammals or lateral line of amphibians have found that CGRP plays an excitatory role.
source: Complicating this hypothesis, most studies on the effects of CGRP in the inner ear of mammals or lateral line of amphibians have found that CGRP plays an excitatory role (Bailey and Sewell, 2000a; Sewell and Starr, 1991; Bailey and Sewell, 2000b; Maison et al., 2003b; Le Prell et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Infusions of CGRP into the guinea pig cochlea increase the amplitude of compound action potentials (CAPs).
source: Infusions of CGRP into the guinea pig cochlea increase the amplitude of compound action potentials (CAPs) (Le Prell et al., 2021)—a measure of bulk SGN activity—whereas CGRP knock-out mice exhibit decreased auditory brainstem response (ABR) amplitudes (Maison et al., 2003b), reinforcing the idea that CGRP enhances SGN firing.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The Ucn receptor Crhr1 is expressed in cochlear supporting cells.
source: In support of this idea, the Ucn receptor Crhr1 is expressed in cochlear supporting cells, suggesting that they may be an alternate target of LOC signaling (Graham and Vetter, 2011; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: NPY and CGRP are both immune-modulatory molecules that could alter inflammatory responses after acoustic injury.
source: Immune cells are another possible target of LOC peptide release, as NPY and CGRP are both immune-modulatory molecules that could alter inflammatory responses after acoustic injury (Assas et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations.
